edges.rationale: Playing one hand alone is the hands-separate practice step put into action.
Playing one hand alone is the hands-separate practice step put into action.
Putting the hands together is the step that hands-separate practice prepares for.
Each hand keeps its own rhythm because melody and accompaniment are separate layers.
A figure shared by the hands is a texture where one line passes from hand to hand.
An even, light accompaniment is what lets the melody stand out above it.
Holding a slow tempo steady is what slow practice asks for.
Building tempo is the second half of slow practice: speed rises only as far as accuracy holds.
The tempo marking sets the speed that building tempo aims for.
Sight-reading at the keys is the strategy of scanning, keeping the pulse and reading ahead put to work.
Playing through without stopping is keeping going in performance, done at the keys.
Playing from memory relies on how the piece was memorised.
Coming in on an upbeat is reading an anacrusis and placing it in time.
Making the hands land together is the core of playing hands together.
Playing hands together nearly always means each hand keeping a different rhythm.
Each hand needs to be secure alone before the two are combined.
Each hand needs to be secure alone before the two are combined.
Playing a piece through means keeping both hands going together from start to finish.
A steady slow tempo is the steady pulse held at practice speed.
An upbeat only lands in time if the pulse is felt before the first note.
Keeping the pulse going matters more in sight-reading than getting every note.
Sight-reading needs each note on the staff to point straight to its key, with no time to name it.
Balancing melody over accompaniment is done with dynamics: one hand softer than the other.
Tempo words sit beside dynamic and articulation marks as the performance directions on a score.
The phrase endings in a piece are where the cadences from harmony are heard.
Repeat signs and endings decide the order the bars of a score are played in.
Binary and ternary are the commonest shapes a score is built from.
Phrases are the smallest units of a score's structure.
Each section of a binary or ternary piece ends with a cadence.
Binary pieces usually mark the repeat of each section with repeat signs.
Chaffin and Imreh found a secure memory is built on the structure of the piece.
The restart points that come from memorising by structure are what let a performer keep going after a slip.
Phrase endings make natural places to start and stop a practice section.
A short section is practised slowly first; small sections and slow tempo work together.
Splitting by hand and splitting by section are both ways to make a hard passage smaller.
The scan before sight-reading is a quick reading of the structure.
A sight-reader checks the tempo marking, then picks a speed they can keep.
Sight-reading and performing share one rule: keep the pulse going after a mistake.
Practice stops to fix a slip while performance keeps going through it, so the two habits pull opposite ways.
Many phrases begin with an upbeat leading into their first strong beat.
Speed is built from a steady slow tempo; raising it before it is steady builds in unevenness.
Hands with different rhythms still have to meet exactly on the beats they share.
Passing a figure between the hands needs the same exact timing as landing together.
Accompaniment patterns usually sit in the left hand.
Both are judged on keeping going: one with new music, the other with music you know.
A memorised performance is a play-through with the score taken away.

items.prompt: What does a double bar line (two thin lines) in the middle of a piece usually mark?

answer.text: The end of a section
answer.explanation: Two thin lines separate one section from the next; the music carries on after them.

wrong.explanation: The final barline is a thin line followed by a thick one; two thin lines mark a section ending inside the piece.
A repeat sign adds two dots beside the barline; without the dots nothing is repeated.
A pause is the fermata sign over a note or rest; a double bar does not stop the pulse.

items.prompt: You scan a 32-bar piece and see that bars 17-24 are the same as bars 1-8. How does that help?

answer.text: There are only 24 bars of new music to learn
answer.explanation: Matching passages are learned once; check the bars where they differ before relying on it.

wrong.text: It does not: every bar has to be learned on its own
wrong.explanation: Repeated bars are the same notes, so learning them twice wastes practice time.

wrong.text: You can leave bars 17-24 out when you play
wrong.explanation: Spotting a repeat saves learning time, not playing time: the bars are still played.
Nothing about returning material changes its tempo.

items.prompt: A repeated passage has a 1st-time bar and a 2nd-time bar. On the second time through, what do you play?

answer.text: Skip the 1st-time bar and play the 2nd-time bar
answer.explanation: The 1st-time bar is only for the first time through; on the repeat you jump straight to the 2nd-time bar.

wrong.explanation: Playing both adds a bar; the 1st-time bar is left out on the repeat.
The 1st-time bar leads back to the repeat, so playing it again would loop a third time.

items.prompt: What does D.C. al Fine tell you to do?

answer.text: Go back to the beginning and play until the word Fine
answer.explanation: Da capo means from the head: back to the start, ending where Fine is written.

wrong.text: Go back to the sign and play until Fine
wrong.explanation: That is D.S. al Fine; dal segno means from the sign, da capo means from the beginning.

wrong.text: Stop here: this is the end
wrong.explanation: The piece does end at Fine, but D.C. sends you back to the start first.
D.C. returns to the very beginning, not to the start of the last section.

items.prompt: A minuet has two sections, each repeated: |: A :|: B :|. What is this form called?

answer.text: Binary form
answer.explanation: Two sections, usually each repeated, make binary form (AB).

wrong.explanation: Ternary form has three sections with the first coming back (ABA); here there are two.
A rondo keeps returning to its main theme between several episodes (ABACA).
Variations restate one theme, changed each time; this piece has two different sections.

items.prompt: In ternary form (ABA), what is true of the last section?

answer.text: It brings back the first section's music
answer.explanation: The second letter A means the opening music returns, often unchanged or nearly so.

wrong.explanation: New music would be labelled C, making ABC; the letter A again means the opening returns.

wrong.text: It is in a different key from the opening
wrong.explanation: The contrasting middle section is the one usually in another key; the returning A comes home.

wrong.text: It is played twice as fast
wrong.explanation: Form describes which music returns, not the tempo.

items.prompt: What is a cadence?

answer.text: The point where a phrase comes to rest
answer.explanation: A cadence closes a phrase, made by its last notes and chords.

wrong.explanation: That is a run, or a cadenza if it is a solo display; a cadence is a resting point.
The speed of the beat is the tempo.

wrong.text: A sign that tells you to repeat
wrong.explanation: That is a repeat sign; a cadence is heard in the music, not written as a sign.

items.prompt: Ode to Joy's first phrase (bars 1-4) ends on the 2nd note of the scale; the second phrase (bars 5-8) ends on the home note. How do the endings feel?

answer.text: The first sounds unfinished, the second sounds finished
answer.explanation: Stopping away from the home note leaves a question; landing on it answers the question.

wrong.explanation: Only the ending on the home note sounds closed; the 2nd note of the scale leans onward.

wrong.text: The first sounds finished, the second unfinished
wrong.explanation: It is the other way round: the home note gives the sense of arrival.

items.prompt: In the opening of Mozart's Sonata K. 545 the left hand plays C-G-E-G over and over under the tune. What is this pattern called?

answer.text: An Alberti bass
answer.explanation: A broken chord played lowest, highest, middle, highest is named after Domenico Alberti.

wrong.explanation: A scale moves by step; this pattern leaps between the notes of one chord.
A trill alternates two neighbouring notes quickly; this pattern uses three chord notes.
A drone holds or repeats one note; this pattern spells out a whole chord.

items.prompt: When one hand plays a melody and the other an accompaniment, which should usually sound louder?

answer.text: The melody
answer.explanation: The accompaniment supports; keeping it lighter lets the tune come through.

wrong.text: The accompaniment, because it has more notes
wrong.explanation: More notes already make it fuller; playing it louder as well buries the tune.
Equal loudness makes the tune hard to pick out; balance puts the melody first.

items.prompt: Which tempo marking is the slowest?

answer.text: Largo
answer.explanation: Largo means broad and very slow.

wrong.explanation: Andante is a walking pace, faster than Largo.
Moderato is moderate, between Andante and Allegro.
Allegro means fast and lively.

items.prompt: A bar is marked rit. and two bars later a tempo. What happens?

answer.text: Slow down gradually, then go back to the original speed
answer.explanation: Ritardando means gradually slower, and a tempo cancels it.

wrong.text: Speed up gradually, then go back to the original speed
wrong.explanation: Speeding up is accel. (accelerando); rit. slows down.
Rit. is gradual, and a tempo returns to the first speed.
Getting quieter is dim. or decresc.; rit. is about speed, not volume.

items.prompt: You keep stumbling in bar 6 at full speed. What is the most useful next step?

answer.text: Play bar 6 slowly enough to get it right every time, then speed up in small steps
answer.explanation: Correct repetitions at a slow tempo build the move; the speed comes back step by step.

wrong.text: Keep playing the whole piece at full speed until it comes
wrong.explanation: Repeating at a speed that causes the slip practises the slip.
Skipping leaves the problem where it is; it will still be there when you perform.

wrong.text: Play bar 6 faster to get through it
wrong.explanation: More speed hides errors and makes them more likely.

items.prompt: Why practise slowly rather than just practising for longer?

answer.text: Slow practice lets you play it right, so the right version is what you repeat
answer.explanation: Duke and colleagues found how pianists practised mattered more than how long they practised.

wrong.explanation: Strength is rarely the limit; the slow tempo helps by giving time to get notes and rhythm right.

wrong.text: Because the piece should be performed slowly too
wrong.explanation: Slow is a practice tempo; you build back up to the marked tempo.

items.prompt: What is the best size of section for fixing a problem spot?

answer.text: A short section around the mistake, starting a little before it
answer.explanation: Starting just before the slip practises the move into it as well as the hard notes.

wrong.text: The whole piece from the start
wrong.explanation: Going back to bar 1 spends most of the time on bars you can already play.
A note on its own misses the move into and out of it; include the notes either side.

items.prompt: You played a wrong note in bar 12. What did the best practisers in research on pianists do at a moment like this?

answer.text: Stopped, found exactly where and why it went wrong, and fixed it before going on
answer.explanation: In Duke and colleagues' study, the best practisers dealt with errors at once and at their source.

wrong.text: Kept going and hoped it would improve next time
wrong.explanation: Errors left alone tend to repeat and become habits.

wrong.text: Started the piece again from the beginning
wrong.explanation: Restarting puts many bars between you and the problem before you reach it again.

items.prompt: When is practising hands separately most useful?

answer.text: When one hand's part has notes or rhythms of its own to learn
answer.explanation: Taking the other hand away lets you learn the hard part without extra demands.

wrong.text: Always, until each hand is perfect through the whole piece
wrong.explanation: Playing together is its own skill; the best practisers in Duke and colleagues' study put hands together early.
Separating the hands is a quick way into a part that is hard on its own.

items.prompt: Each hand works alone, but together they fall apart. What helps most?

answer.text: Play hands together much slower, a short section at a time
answer.explanation: Coordination is the new skill, and only practising together at a speed you can manage trains it.

wrong.text: Practise each hand alone some more
wrong.explanation: Each hand already works; separate practice does not teach the hands to line up.

wrong.text: Play together at full speed until it works
wrong.explanation: At full speed the same mistakes repeat; slow down so the hands line up.
Loudness does not change when the notes are played.

items.prompt: You have half a minute to look at a piece before sight-reading it. What should you check first?

answer.text: The key signature, time signature and tempo
answer.explanation: These change every note and every bar; getting them wrong spoils the whole reading.

wrong.text: The hardest bar, practising it until it is perfect
wrong.explanation: There is no time to practise; a scan of the whole piece prevents more mistakes.
There is no time for every note; the key and time signature matter more.
The ending tells you little about which notes and pulse to start with.

items.prompt: While sight-reading, where should your eyes be?

answer.text: A little ahead of the notes you're playing
answer.explanation: Skilled readers look ahead, so they can prepare each note before it is due.

wrong.explanation: Looking down loses your place on the page; find the keys by feel.

wrong.text: Exactly on the note you are playing
wrong.explanation: Then you see each note only as it is due, too late to prepare it.

items.prompt: While sight-reading you play a wrong note. What should you do?

answer.text: Keep the pulse and carry on
answer.explanation: Sight-reading is judged on a steady, continuous reading; stopping breaks the rhythm.

wrong.text: Stop and replay the bar correctly
wrong.explanation: Going back loses the pulse and costs more than the wrong note did.
Changing tempo midway breaks the pulse; choose a tempo at the start that you can keep.

items.prompt: Which way of memorising a piece holds up best under pressure?

answer.text: Knowing its structure: sections, phrases and where things change
answer.explanation: Chaffin and Imreh found an expert pianist built her memory on the formal structure, which gave her places to restart.

wrong.text: Repeating it until your fingers know it
wrong.explanation: Finger memory alone is quick but fragile: if it slips, there is no way back in mid-piece.
Seeing the page helps alongside other kinds of memory, but alone it leaves no backup.

items.prompt: Why practise starting from different places in a memorised piece, not just the beginning?

answer.text: So that after a slip you can pick up at the next section
answer.explanation: Several secure starting points mean a slip costs a few notes, not the whole piece.

wrong.text: Because the beginning is always the hardest part
wrong.explanation: The beginning is not usually the hardest; the point is to have more than one way in.

wrong.text: It does not help; always start at the beginning
wrong.explanation: Only starting at bar 1 means a slip in the middle sends you all the way back.

items.prompt: In a performance you lose your place in bar 10. What is the best recovery?

answer.text: Come back in, in time, at the next beat or bar you know
answer.explanation: Keeping the pulse in your head and rejoining keeps the slip small.

wrong.text: Start the piece again from the beginning
wrong.explanation: Restarting makes the slip much bigger for the listener.

wrong.text: Stop and wait until you remember
wrong.explanation: Silence breaks the music and the pulse with it.

items.prompt: How is practising different from performing?

answer.text: In practice you stop to fix mistakes; in performance you keep going
answer.explanation: Each has its job: practice repairs errors, performance carries the music through them.

wrong.text: There is no difference: never stop in practice either
wrong.explanation: Practice that never stops leaves errors unfixed; stopping to fix them is what practice is for.
Nerves usually push you faster already; play at a tempo you have practised.

items.prompt: A piece in 4/4 begins with a single crotchet before the first full bar. What is that note called?

answer.text: An anacrusis (upbeat)
answer.explanation: Notes before the first full bar are an anacrusis; they lead into its first beat.

wrong.explanation: A grace note is a small ornamental note attached to a main note.
A tie is a curved line joining two notes of the same pitch.
A rest is a silence; this is a note that is played.

items.prompt: A piece in 4/4 begins with a one-beat upbeat. On which beat of the bar does that note fall?

answer.text: Beat 4
answer.explanation: The upbeat fills the last beat of an incomplete bar, so beat 1 arrives with the first full bar.

wrong.explanation: Beat 1 is the first note of the first full bar, straight after the upbeat.
A one-beat upbeat in 4/4 takes the last beat, not the second.
The upbeat is part of the pulse: count 1, 2, 3 silently and play on 4.
